modules.title: Classes and Object-Oriented Programming
modules.description: Learn how to create your own types with classes, bundle data and behavior together, and design programs using object-oriented principles.

sections.heading: Learning Objectives
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
1. Define a class using the class keyword
2. Create an __init__ method to initialize instances
3. Understand the self parameter
4. Create instance variables and methods
5. Instantiate objects from a class

sections.heading: What is a Class?
sections.body: A class is a blueprint for creating objects. It bundles data (attributes) and functions (methods) together. Creating a new class creates a new type of object.
sections.code:
# Define a class
class Student:
    """A simple Student class."""
    
    def __init__(self, name, grade):
        """Initialize a new student."""
        self.name = name      # instance attribute
        self.grade = grade    # instance attribute
    
    def introduce(self):
        """Return a greeting string."""
        return f'Hi, I am {self.name} and I am in grade {self.grade}'

# Create instances (objects)
s1 = Student('Maria', 10)
s2 = Student('Juan', 9)

print(s1.introduce())  # Hi, I am Maria and I am in grade 10
print(s2.introduce())  # Hi, I am Juan and I am in grade 9

sections.heading: The __init__ Method
sections.body: The __init__ method is the constructor — it's called automatically when you create a new instance. The first parameter is always self.
sections.code:
class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, author, pages):
        self.title = title
        self.author = author
        self.pages = pages
        self.current_page = 0  # default value
    
    def read(self, pages):
        self.current_page += pages
        if self.current_page > self.pages:
            self.current_page = self.pages
        print(f'Read to page {self.current_page}')

book = Book('Python 101', 'Maria', 200)
book.read(50)   # Read to page 50
book.read(30)   # Read to page 80
print(book.title)  # Python 101

sections.heading: Instance Variables vs Class Variables
sections.body: Instance variables are unique to each object. Class variables are shared across all instances.
sections.code:
class Dog:
    # Class variable — shared by all dogs
    species = 'Canis familiaris'
    
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        # Instance variables — unique per dog
        self.name = name
        self.age = age
    
    def description(self):
        return f'{self.name} is {self.age} years old'

d1 = Dog('Buddy', 3)
d2 = Dog('Luna', 5)

print(d1.species)  # Canis familiaris
print(d2.species)  # Canis familiaris (shared)
print(d1.description())  # Buddy is 3 years old

# Override class variable on instance
Dog.species = 'Canis lupus'  # changes for ALL instances

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

2. Override methods in the subclass
3. Use super() to call the parent's methods
4. Understand isinstance() checks
5. Explain the concept of inheritance

sections.heading: Basic Inheritance
sections.body: Inheritance lets you define a new class that reuses, extends, or modifies the behavior of an existing class.

sections.heading: Using super()
sections.body: Use super() to call the parent class's methods, especially in __init__ to set up inherited attributes.

sections.heading: Checking Types with isinstance()
sections.body: Use isinstance() to check whether an object is an instance of a particular class (or its subclasses).
sections.code:
class Animal: pass
class Dog(Animal): pass
class Cat(Animal): pass

d = Dog()
c = Cat()

print(isinstance(d, Dog))     # True
print(isinstance(d, Animal))  # True (Dog IS an Animal)
print(isinstance(c, Dog))     # False
print(type(d) == Dog)         # True (but doesn't check inheritance)

sections.heading: When to Use Inheritance
sections.body:
Inheritance is powerful but easy to overuse. The test: is the child a true specialised version of the parent? Dog IS AN Animal, Circle IS A Shape — those work. But a Car HAS AN Engine: that is composition (the car stores an engine object), not inheritance. Confusing the two leads to tangled code.

In PyKnowledge-style apps, inheritance appears everywhere: a QuizQuestion parent with MultipleChoiceQuestion and FillBlank children; each child stores different data but shares the same checking logic.

Rule of thumb for beginners: inherit only when the child can stand in for the parent anywhere in your program. If you find yourself deleting or overriding most of the parent's behaviour, inheritance was probably the wrong choice.

sections.heading: Learning Objectives
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
1. Understand Python's iterator protocol (__iter__, __next__)
2. Create custom iterators by implementing the protocol
3. Write generator functions using yield
4. Use generator expressions
5. Explain how for loops work under the hood

sections.heading: The Iterator Protocol
sections.body: Python's for loop works by calling iter() on an object to get an iterator, then calling next() repeatedly until StopIteration is raised.

sections.heading: Creating a Custom Iterator
sections.body: Any class with __iter__() and __next__() methods is an iterator. __iter__() returns self. __next__() either returns the next value or raises StopIteration.

sections.heading: Generator Functions
sections.body: A generator is a function that uses yield instead of return. Each time yield is reached, the function pauses and resumes from that point on the next call.
sections.code:
def countdown(n):
    while n > 0:
        yield n
        n -= 1

# Using the generator
for num in countdown(5):
    print(num, end=' ')  # 5 4 3 2 1

print()

# Convert to list
print(list(countdown(3)))  # [3, 2, 1]

# Generators are memory-efficient for large sequences
# because they yield one item at a time

sections.heading: Generator Expressions
sections.body: Generator expressions are like list comprehensions but with parentheses instead of brackets. They produce values on demand rather than building the entire list.
sections.code:
# Generator expression for filtering
# Find first 5 even squares
gen = (x**2 for x in range(100) if x**2 % 2 == 0)
first_5 = [next(gen) for _ in range(5)]
print(first_5)  # [0, 4, 16, 36, 64]

exercises.explanation: The generator yields 1, then 2, then 3 in sequence. list() consumes all values.
